title: Context-Aware Cooperative Gating for Knowledge-Controlled Value Factorization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability requires decentralized agents to act from incomplete local information. Value-decomposition methods such as VDN and QMIX do not control when teammate-related knowledge may influence an agent’s local utility, and an uncontrolled teammate-conditioned term can distort decisions at timesteps where no ally is observable. We propose CA-QMIX, a context-aware value factorization method that uses ally visibility as a knowledge signal for decentralized agent control. Each agent combines an individual decision branch with an attention-based cooperative knowledge branch through a visibility-conditioned gate that scales the cooperative contribution and is hard-masked to zero when no ally is observable. The gated utilities are combined by a QMIX-style monotonic mixer, which we prove preserves Individual-Global-Max consistency, and a mixer-level Δ-Q regularizer discourages cooperative corrections that lower the greedy value of the base branch. Experiments on seven SMAC v1 and SMAC v2 scenarios against six value-decomposition baselines show that CA-QMIX attains the highest mean final win rate and the best mean rank over the seven scenarios and improves on QMIX in all three randomized SMAC v2 scenarios. Ablations show that most of the gain comes from the cooperative branch, that its visibility conditioning helps when correctly aligned (misaligned visibility degrades performance under randomized placement), and that the form of the gate is not critical: a binary gate suffices and the hard no-ally mask has no measurable cost.

title: Measuring Mechanistic Uncertainty in Large Language Models via Causal Robustness
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.

title: Temporal Periodic Image Registration with Implicit Neural Representations
abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have recently gained popularity for their ability to model functions using simple and lightweight networks. These methods have also proven effective in deformable image registration. In this work, we extend INRs for deformable image registration to the domain of temporal image registration, focusing on periodic temporal image sequences. Our approach, Temporal-IDIR, optimizes a single INR to model deformations across all frames in a temporal image sequence simultaneously, allowing for self-regularization through its own deformation predictions. To achieve this, we introduce a temporal consistency loss that penalizes discrepancies between direct source-to-target transformations and those traversing intermediate frames. We evaluate our framework on the DIR-LAB dataset, using the target registration error (TRE) between annotated and moved landmarks as the metric. Here, we achieve a TRE of 1.03 mm, outperforming other INR-based registration methods. Additionally, our framework supports smooth interpolation between time frames by estimating deformations between the given input frames. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MMLowes/Temporal_INR.

title: RoPE-Flow: Monocular Vision-based Robot Pose Estimation via 2D Graph-Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app

title: Leveraging Large Language Model Token Probabilities for Literature Review Abstract Filtering
abstract: Grasping the latest knowledge in any field has become increasingly challenging given the rapid pace of modern publishing. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly embedding models and large language models (LLMs), provide promising tools to aid researchers in the filtration and identification of the most relevant literature. However, there is little practical guidance on how to incorporate LLMs into literature reviews, and there are not yet direct comparisons of embedding models versus generative approaches. In this work, we compare these methods using small local LLMs for literature screening on both a simple dataset containing distinct categories and a more complex example with abstracts obtained from the Web of Science. We find that embedding models perform strongly for simple, well-separated queries due to their robustness and computational efficiency. For more complex filtering tasks, generative approaches based on token probabilities can achieve competitive or superior performance, but only when properly calibrated and when token-level outputs are interpreted as continuous scores rather than binary decisions. However, we show these methods are highly sensitive to prompt formulation, token conventions, and threshold selection.

title: Does Grounding Argument Strengths in Evidence Text Help Claim Verification? A Study of Token-Anchored Arguments vs. ArgRAG
abstract: This paper investigates whether grounding argument strengths in evidence text improves automated claim verification. Building on ArgRAG, the study introduces the Token Argument Model (TAM), which represents retrieved evidence as shorter arguments anchored to verbatim text and estimates argument strength using a Natural Language Inference (NLI) model. TAM is evaluated across four experimental settings using PubHealth and SciFact. Results show that grounding argument strengths does not consistently improve claim-verification accuracy over uniform argument strengths, and randomly shuffled strength scores achieve comparable results. However, representing evidence as shorter, quote-anchored arguments improves accuracy by 6.0 percentage points on PubHealth in the top-5 retrieval setting. The findings suggest that improving argument representation can be more beneficial than assigning model-derived strength scores. Reproducibility note: The reproduced ArgRAG baseline does not match the accuracy reported in the original paper. Results should therefore be interpreted as relative comparisons within this experimental setup, not as direct comparisons with the original benchmark performance.

title: A Hybrid RAG-Based Framework for Improved Information Retrieval from Long Documents via Summarization and Question Answering
abstract: We present an integrated system, which is a mix of summarization as well as Question Answering (QA) to boost the performance regarding information retrieval (IR) for long and domain-intensive documents. This work creates a synergistic relationship between both tasks to enhance retrieval efficiency and quality of answers, unlike previous studies focusing separately on either summarization or QA. The framework proposed is comprised of three stages. First, it involves summarization that is used for condensing documents, maintaining their key semantic content. Second, it employs a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture, where the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model is used for the retrieval stage, while T5 and BART-Large-CNN models are utilized for the generation stage. Lastly, answers generated are put into comparison with a baseline system which works with complete document processing without summarization. Results at the NIPS dataset reveal that integrating summarization with QA significantly improves each summary informativeness and answer accuracy. To investigate the impact of summarization inside the retrieval pipeline, two complementary eventualities are explored. First, Proactive Summarization as an Indexing Tool (Summarization-First) plays summarization earlier than the indexing and retrieval stages to reduce record size and improve retrieval performance while keeping semantic relevance. Second, Query-Guided Contextual Summarization (Retrieval-First Summarization) applies summarization after the retrieval level, wherein only the retrieved relevant passages are summarized in step with consumer question for generating more targeted and context-conscious solutions. These two scenarios enable a comparative analysis of the way the position of summarization within RAG pipeline impacts retrieval efficiency as well as solution era quality. title: AEDS: Adaptive edge‐difference shaping for piecewise‐stationary sparse‐reward reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract Sparse‐reward tasks with piecewise‐stationary topology shifts challenge reinforcement learning. Continuous spectral shaping biases agents toward geometric extrema and can delay adaptation when bottlenecks move. We propose adaptive edge‐difference shaping (AEDS), a spectral reward‐shaping method that focuses exploration on structural bottlenecks. AEDS triggers a direction‐agnostic intrinsic reward only when the agent crosses the sign‐flip boundary of the dynamically updated Fiedler vector. An episodic gating mechanism limits rewarded crossings and bounds the cumulative intrinsic return. Within each stationary phase, AEDS induces an augmented Markov decision process to which the standard tabular Q‐learning convergence theorem applies. We evaluate AEDS on grid environments with shifting bottlenecks and geometric traps. Across the evaluation, AEDS performs strongly in several bottleneck‐oriented settings, while count‐based exploration or well‐oriented dense spectral shaping can be preferable in other regimes. These results support a focused scope for AEDS in bottleneck‐oriented sparse‐reward grid tasks.

title: Oblivis: A Framework for Delegated and Efficient Oblivious Transfer
abstract: As database deployments shift toward cloud platforms and edge devices, thin clients need to securely retrieve sensitive records without leaking their query intent or metadata to the proxies that mediate access. Oblivious Transfer (OT) is a core tool for private retrieval, yet existing OTs assume direct client–database interaction and lack support for delegated querying or lightweight clients. We present Oblivis, a modular framework of new OT protocols that enable delegated, privacy-preserving query execution. Oblivis allows clients to retrieve database records without direct access, protects against leakage to both databases and proxies, and is designed with practical efficiency in mind. Its components include: (1) Delegated-Query OT, which permits secure outsourcing of query generation; (2) Multi-Receiver OT for merged, cloud-hosted databases; (3) a compiler producing constant-size responses suitable for thin clients; and (4) Supersonic OT, a proxy-based, information- theoretic, and highly efficient 1-out-of-2 OT. The protocols are formally defined and proven secure in the simulation-based paradigm, under non-colluding assumption. We implement and empirically evaluate Supersonic OT. It achieves at least a 92× speedup over a highly efficient 1-out-of-2 OT, and a 2.6×–106× speedup over a standard OT extension across 200–100,000 invocations. Our implementation further shows that Supersonic OT remains efficient even on constrained hardware, e.g., it completes an end-to-end transfer in 1.36 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4.

title: People and algorithms: Working with AI in marketing
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is no longer a distant technological trend in marketing. Used well, AI can boost marketing practice. Without an informed, critical approach to use, it can reproduce bias, generate misleading insights, weaken creativity, and create serious ethical, legal, and security risks. This handbook has been prepared to support your work with Artificial Intelligence in marketing in a thoughtful, creative, and responsible way. Its goal is not only to introduce AI tools and concepts, but also to help you develop the judgment required to use them effectively. The handbook is primarily addressed to marketing students at the master’s level. It has been devel­oped by marketing departments from European universities who are witnessing how AI the trans­formation of the profession and deciding how marketing education should respond to this change. The chapters are designed to connect conceptual understanding with practical application, helping students prepare for marketing roles in which AI will be part of everyday work. This handbook is the result of collaboration between academics from Poznań University of Econom­ics and Business (Poland, project leader) and Corvinus University of Budapest (Hungary), University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria, Stockholm School of Economics (Sweden), Complutense Universi­ty of Madrid (Spain), Polytechnic University of Marche, Ancona (Italy), University of Zagreb, Faculty of Economicsand Business (Croatia), and University of Perpignan (France). This handbook has been supported by the Polish National Agency for Academic Exchange under the NAWA Strategic Partnership program, project BNI/PST/2023/1/00082 DIGIT: People and algorithms in organisations.

title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.

title: Physics-Aware Distillation of a Grid Foundation Model for Real-Time Edge Inference
abstract: Grid foundation models (GridFMs) are graph transformers pretrained on a masked power-flow objective, and evaluate power flow orders of magnitude faster than an iterative solver. Their size, however, targets data-centre inference, whereas low-inertia operation increasingly asks for inference at the edge, next to the measurement, at batch size one and within a single synchrophasor (PMU) reporting frame. We distil a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer GridFM teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student, a $32.5\times$ parameter reduction at half the message-passing depth, using an objective that combines the masked power-flow loss with output, physics-residual, latent-state and attention transfer. The physics-residual term, which matches the teacher's power-residual profile, has not previously been applied to typed power-grid graphs. We evaluate on a renewable variant of the IEEE 118-bus benchmark grid in which 26 of the conventional (synchronous) generators are replaced by inverter-based renewables with battery flexibility and standardised reactive-power limits (IEEE 1547), giving $97\,529$ physically valid (AC-OPF-feasible) operating scenarios, and we ablate all eight combinations of the transfer terms, reporting accuracy against ground truth and fidelity to the teacher separately. Distillation lowers student error on all four predicted quantities, by up to $48\%$ on active-power dispatch, and every distilled student is more accurate than its teacher on reactive-power dispatch. The gain is largely carried by the output matching term. The physics-residual term, in the layer-aggregated form used here, is consistently harmful, which we attribute to the spatial averaging it applies to a bus-level residual field. The resulting student is $32.5\times$ smaller in parameter count and has half the message-passing depth, making it a candidate for subsequent edge-device benchmarking.

title: Rethinking Classifier-Free Guidance for TI2I Flow Matching
abstract: We study Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) flow matching methods for controllable image editing. In a broader generative modeling context, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is established as a key component responsible for high quality outputs. However, we argue that its role in TI2I modeling is poorly understood. Specifically, we make the surprising observation that the CFG mechanism is implicitly harmful for editing in the noisy phase of flow modeling, hindering instruction following and controllability. We propose a simple correction in the early flow steps, enabling a richer alignment-preservation tradeoff at no extra cost. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on both pixel-space and latent TI2I flows.

title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation in S3-Compatible Object Storage under Client Concurrency
abstract: Data encrypted today with classical public-key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client-side encryption that protects it must move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM, which adds a key-encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML-KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML-KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single-node store and one cloud provider.

title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG
abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. On SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods give the generator 0.7K to 2.7K visual tokens per query on average under a common image processor, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. At a fixed 16K budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input. We study what the generator needs from retrieved pages through two requirements: Loud, making full use of visual token capacity, and Clear, refining the page so that its evidence becomes prominent. For Loud, increasing either the visual token budget or visual fidelity, the image resolution those tokens preserve, improves accuracy with the other held fixed, and full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets. For Clear, suppressing surrounding content improves accuracy without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of these regions to page images outperforms either input alone. We implement both as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or additional training. LoC outperforms eight prior methods on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, improving over the strongest, ColQwen3, by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points with the same retriever and generator. It also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget. These results locate a bottleneck beyond retrieval: how the retrieved pages are given to the generator.

title: Does Zero-Edit Practice Support a Claim to Human Authorship?
abstract: This article examines whether meaningful human authorship can survive full post-generation delegation to a generative AI system: a condition in which a human originates a concept, directs and iterates on its generation, evaluates and selects a result, but performs no subsequent modification of the output. The author’s earlier article, cited in the references, proposed a five-dimension agency framework for evaluating Zero-Edit practice. The present article takes a different approach: it examines the authorship question through five external approaches (Deng; Anscomb; Fritz; Militsyna; Huang et al.), none of which was developed with full post-generation delegation as its central case. These approaches are not treated as equivalent tests: Anscomb supplies a theoretical analogy, while the others are assessed according to their distinct analytical aims. The analysis applies these approaches to the author’s own Zero-Edit practice as a boundary case, using primary sources rather than secondary summaries. It distinguishes creative agency, expressive control, and execution; engages two substantial counterarguments through first-person case evidence; and tests the practice against one of its own weaker instances, allowing that case to count against the thesis where warranted. The case does not establish authorship under any single framework. evidence.abstract: This article examines whether meaningful human authorship can survive full post-generation delegation to a generative AI system: a condition in which a human originates a concept, directs and iterates on its generation, evaluates and selects a result, but performs no subsequent modification of the output. title: No Poker Face: Why AI Can't Keep the Answer to Itself
abstract: Preprint (v1.1) of “No Poker Face: Why AI Can’t Keep the Answer to Itself” by Vijay Suresh, with the full data and code release. Learners increasingly ask AI models to write practice questions. A practice question is only useful if answering it requires the knowledge it tests. This paper studies clue leakage: properties of a question, other than the tested knowledge, that let someone answer it. Following earlier work on fictional subjects, it uses invented subjects that no model can know, so any accuracy above chance by a solver without the study material is leakage. Main pre-registered study (168 seven-round study sessions, 11,760 questions, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol as writers): neither confirmatory hypothesis was supported. Writers did not make sets easier after heavy reported failure, and none declared a learner ready on an unsupported mastery claim (0/24 vs 0/24). But a solver with no study material answered about half of all questions correctly (chance 25%), and asking for harder questions made them longer and more guessable, not harder. Pre-registered confirmatory follow-up (112 sessions, two new invented subjects): difficulty requests raised no-material accuracy by +5.9 points (95% CI 1.9 to 9.5, one-sided p = 0.002). An instruction to make wrong options as long and specific as the correct one removed the “longest option is correct” cue (37.6% → 25.6%) but did not reduce leakage (+2.2 points, p = 0.95). Removing the visible cue does not remove the leak. A 28-session Gemini 3.1 Pro arm and a real learner’s exam-prep sessions (case study) show the same patterns. Pre-registrations: osf.io/uya5q (main), osf.io/93vpn (Addendum 1), osf.io/3z64e (Addendum 2). Code: github.com/vjgits/research-papers. The zip contains transcripts, item-level solver results, per-call cost ledgers, analysis outputs, independent recomputation scripts and a log of every AI error made while running the study. Human-coder validation will follow in v1.2.

title: YSP0Github/SeisY-Releases: SeisY v0.1.10
abstract: SeisY 0.1.10 更新说明 发布日期:2026-10-15 本版本为问题修复与稳定性增强版本,重点修复了部分用户安装 0.1.9 后无法启动的问题,并系统排查、消除了同类隐患。 一、关键修复:无 G 盘电脑启动崩溃 问题现象:部分用户安装 0.1.9 后首次启动即报错退出: Failed to execute script 'gui' due to unhandled exception: FileNotFoundError: [WinError 3] 系统找不到指定的路径。: 'G:\\' 根本原因:安装包内随包分发的 Config.ini 残留了开发机的工作目录配置(work_dir = G:\...)。程序启动时会自动创建该工作目录,当用户电脑上没有 G 盘时,os.makedirs 直接失败,程序在主界面出现前崩溃。 修复内容: 启动目录自动回退:配置中的工作目录若指向不存在的盘符(如 G:\、H:\),自动切换到用户主目录下的 SeisY_Projects 文件夹,并在启动后给出一次性提示,告知用户新的工作目录位置。 全路径校验:缓存目录、数据保存目录、Apollo 数据库目录、仪器响应文件等路径同样做盘符校验,无效时自动重建或清空,避免后续功能再因同类问题报错。 清理出厂配置:随包分发的 Config.ini 已移除所有开发机绝对路径,工作目录、缓存、数据库等均在首次启动时于用户目录下自动创建。 升级后工作目录默认为:C:\Users\<你的用户名>\SeisY_Projects,可在「配置 → 修改配置」中随时修改。 二、其他健壮性改进 Apollo 月震数据库:配置指向不存在盘符时,自动回退到用户目录下的 database,不再依赖开发机路径。 批量去异常 / 双库对比查看器:默认数据库路径改为用户主目录,不再写死 G:\SeisY_Project\...。 月球昼夜分布图、3D 地球、测试数据浏览等功能中的贴图与起始目录改为相对程序目录解析,不再依赖固定盘符。 新增 12 项回归测试(路径盘符防护),覆盖"缺失盘符启动""配置二次加载校验""出厂配置守护"等场景,防止该问题复发。 三、0.1.9 老用户临时解决办法(不升级也可) 若暂时无法升级,可手动删除安装目录下的配置文件后重启,程序会自动重建: C:\Users\<用户名>\AppData\Local\Programs\SeisY\_internal\seisy\Config.ini 直接安装 0.1.10 即可覆盖解决,无需手动处理。 校验信息 安装包:SeisY-0.1.10-Setup.exe(约 818 MB) SHA-256: 2C959BDE89087AB2B6E347F3763E632B2E14B9E81BEAF04F4D4074ACAFEABF4F 也可下载随附的 SeisY-0.1.10-SHA256.txt 核对。

title: Diagnosing Unconditional Migration in the Snow Ablation Optimizer Through Controlled Retention Strategies
abstract: The Snow Ablation Optimizer (SAO) uses ranked solutions to generate candidates but accepts every evaluated candidate, even when it degrades its source state. We examined whether this unconditional migration rule created a systematic risk for the individuals that contributed most to search progress. On 12 representative CEC2017 functions, current leaders produced a median 82.51% of generation-best improvements. Their median candidate-degradation rate was 64.26%, compared with 35.72% for followers, and the difference remained significant on all functions after Holm correction. This contribution–risk concentration identifies candidate acceptance and protection target as the relevant correction points. A unified retention rule compared fitness-ranked leader retention (LR), random retention (R), full retention (ALL), and the original SAO without changing candidate generation or the evaluation budget. A 30-seed, five-percentage-point diagnostic grid selected LR-70% and nominal R-95% for the complete benchmark. Across 84 CEC2017 and CEC2022 function–dimension blocks and 19 algorithms, R-95% achieved the lowest overall mean-error rank (3.0476). Its global rank was better than every comparator after Holm correction, including LR-70% and ALL. Median-error ranking and exclusion of CEC2017 F2 preserved this CEC result.

title: Advanced Digital Signature Schemes for Blockchain Systems
abstract: It discusses about the advanced digital signature techniques that were specifically designed to cater to the needs of modern blockchain systems concerning scalability, privacy, and efficiency. Through the study of aggregate signatures, particularly the BLS scheme, the aim is to comprehend the process of reducing numerous signatures into one verifiable proof. Subsequently, the chapter touches on group signatures and ring signatures, revealing how they offer anonymity of the signers while ensuring accountability and verifiability. Blind signatures are scrutinized regarding their importance in privacy-centric applications like anonymous payments and voting. Proxy signatures are introduced as a technique for managing the signing authority delegation in decentralized workflows. For all the schemes, the reader is introduced to the mathematical intuition, security assumptions, and practical deployment issues. A comparative analysis at the end of the chapter facilitates the selection of the suitable signature schemes depending on the performance, privacy, and trust requirements in a given blockchain environment.

title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
abstract: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
abstract: We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.

title: On the Complexity of Finding Stationary Points in Stochastic $(L_0, L_1)$-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: We study the stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity of finding $ε$-stationary points of $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth nonconvex functions. Under bounded-variance noise, existing analyses of normalized and clipped stochastic gradient descent (SGD) establish optimal dependence on $ε$ and $L_0$, but the jointly optimal dependence on $L_0$, $L_1$, and $ε$ remains unclear. We resolve this question for an unbiased SFO whose gradient noise has a $p$th central moment bounded by $σ^p$ for some $σ\geq 0$, where $p\in(1,2]$.Specifically, we establish an SFO lower bound of $Ω\big(\big(σ^{\frac{p}{p-1}}ε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}+1\big) (L_0 Δε^{-2}+L_1Δε^{-1})\big)$, where $Δ>0$ is the initial optimality gap.This bound identifies an unavoidable contribution proportional to $L_1ε^{-1}Δ$. We also prove that mini-batch (smoothed) normalized SGD can attain a matching upper bound, thereby establishing the optimal SFO complexity.

title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. A preliminary evaluation with children aged 8-10 combined interaction logs, post-task ratings, and semi-structured interviews. The findings suggest that Agent style shaped children's engagement and response pathways: partner-like interaction tended to support direct questioning, while tool-like interaction was more associated with evidence seeking. Children generally viewed AI as useful but fallible, and their questioning behaviors varied in reasoning depth. The study contributes design insights for supporting children's critical, reflective, and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.

title: Amora: Communication-Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbors search (ANNS) over cloud-hosted vector databases raises a critical privacy concern: the query vector, which often encodes sensitive user intent, is exposed to the server. Private ANNS (PANNS) allows a client to retrieve nearest neighbors without revealing its query. The state-of-the-art single-server scheme, Pacmann (ICLR'25), achieves high accuracy via graph-based search with private information retrieval (PIR), but incurs substantial communication overhead because each PIR query retrieves only a single vertex. We present Amora, a communication-efficient PANNS system that applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index so that one PIR query is amortized over many vertices. To retrieve as much of the distance and neighbor information the search needs under a limited communication budget, Amora adopts a dual-PIR split layout with two heterogeneous PIR matrices that stay balanced in dimension: VecPIR retrieves inner products for an entire partition of vertices as their distance at once, while NbrPIR retrieves necessary neighbor lists at subgroup granularity for graph traversal. This layout shifts the cost model of PIR query from per-vertex to per-partition, which significantly reduces the communication overhead. To further improve efficiency by reducing the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database, Amora introduces batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication, centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions, and TopCand exploration that seeds jump-style graph navigation with the closest vertices from each retrieved partition. We evaluate Amora on five datasets spanning 96 to 1024 dimensions and up to 10 million vectors. Compared to Pacmann, Amora reduces online communication by 93--99% while achieving higher search accuracy.

The state-of-the-art single-server scheme, Pacmann (ICLR'25), achieves high accuracy via graph-based search with private information retrieval (PIR), but incurs substantial communication overhead because each PIR query retrieves only a single vertex. We present Amora, a communication-efficient PANNS system that applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index so that one PIR query is amortized over many vertices. To retrieve as much of the distance and neighbor information the search needs under a limited communication budget, Amora adopts a dual-PIR split layout with two heterogeneous PIR matrices that stay balanced in dimension: VecPIR retrieves inner products for an entire partition of vertices as their distance at once, while NbrPIR retrieves necessary neighbor lists at subgroup granularity for graph traversal. This layout shifts the cost model of PIR query from per-vertex to per-partition, which significantly reduces the communication overhead. To further improve efficiency by reducing the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database, Amora introduces batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication, centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions, and TopCand exploration that seeds jump-style graph navigation with the closest vertices from each retrieved partition. We evaluate Amora on five datasets spanning 96 to 1024 dimensions and up to 10 million vectors. Compared to Pacmann, Amora reduces online communication by 93--99% while achieving higher search accuracy.

title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.

title: Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
abstract: Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.

title: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Before Post-Training: An End-to-End Approach
abstract: Agentic capabilities are increasingly important for modern LLMs, yet remain difficult to evaluate during pretraining. Existing approaches typically rely on static trajectory-derived tasks or likelihood-based proxies, which are lightweight but provide limited visibility into how base models behave in interactive environments. We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for eliciting and evaluating agentic behavior from pretrained base models on end-to-end tasks. Rather than converting base models into chat-style agents, ASAP preserves the completion interface and adapts existing agent scaffolds through structured trajectory continuation, short reference prefixes, and minimal recovery mechanisms. Across software-engineering and deep-research benchmarks, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance across base models and pretraining checkpoints. Beyond aggregate scores, ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories, enabling analysis of exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion across training stages. These trajectories provide a behavioral view of how agent-relevant capabilities change during pretraining and how execution patterns differ after post-training. Our results suggest that end-to-end agent evaluation can complement conventional pretraining benchmarks by providing a practical diagnostic of interactive model behavior.

title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
abstract: Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student's behavior with the teacher's. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. At each such state, ActionOPD samples actions from both the student and a black-box teacher, rewarding student actions according to their semantic agreement with the sampled teacher actions. Through policy optimization, ActionOPD aligns the student's action-level behavior with the teacher's decisions without requiring reproduction of teacher-written reasoning or access to teacher token probabilities. Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with two teachers on diverse, curated tool-use tasks yields average gains of 3.3-6.9 percentage points across four out-of-distribution benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability, without requiring the teacher and student to share a model family or tokenizer. On $τ^2$-bench, ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. We further explore Self-ActionOPD with a same-model teacher and privileged context. These results establish ActionOPD as a promising approach to agent distillation.

title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.

title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction

title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.

title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.

title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.

We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.

title: KANLab: TensorFlow Playground for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
abstract: KANLab is a browser-based visualization tool designed to interactively teach the core concepts of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), forked from the widely successful TensorFlow Playground. To maximize educational clarity, KANLab omits residual connections and learnable scaling parameters found in modern KAN implementations, ensuring that displayed B-spline activation curves directly correspond to their underlying trainable control points. Users can inspect and modify activation functions, initialization schemes and observe gradient descent correcting manual disruptions. Furthermore, user can explore phenomena such as activation variance, interactive pruning, and re\-/training within a compact 2D machine learning setting. KANLab is open-source and available at https://kanlab.app/

title: Anuvani-LID: Robust and Calibrated Spoken Language Identification for Indian Languages
abstract: Every multilingual speech pipeline begins with a language decision, an error there propagates silently through recognition, translation and routing. In India it spans 22 scheduled languages across four language families, heard over short, noisy, narrowband and code-mixed audio. Foundational speech models increasingly present language identification (LID) as an inherent latent, generalized capability. Autoregressive decoders in speech models emit a special language ID token, and modern LLMs with audio capabilities can name the language when prompted. We test this assumption on identical clips and find that whisper and similar speech models has tokens for only 15 of the 23 languages, on one second inputs Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.52 macro-F1 and GPT-audio 0.14. We present Anuvani LID, a dedicated 115M parameter LID conformer model trained on 54,643 hours of Indian speech spanning 22 Indian languages and Indian accented English. Along with designed and controlled studies on 102 condition benchmark with speaker and corpus held out tests. Across 37 conditions, it reaches 0.914 mean macro-F1, 5.2 points above Gemini 3.5 Flash and ahead of 14 other systems. It is 24 points ahead of Gemini at one second, scores 0.897 on all 23 languages where no other system exceeds 0.713, and is calibrated to an ECE of 0.008. Reliable Indian LID still requires a robust, dedicated and calibrated model.

title: Anuvani-Diarization: Zero Shot Speaker Diarization and Annotation Conventions Across 22 Languages
abstract: India's 22 scheduled languages are spoken by over a billion people in conversations that mix languages, often within one turn, overlap freely, and take place over telephones, in meetings, and in media. Knowing who spoke when, the task of speaker diarization, is essential to speech applications for such conversation: voice agents conversing with several people at once, speaker attributed transcription of meetings and calls, contact center analytics, and media monitoring. We present a systematic study of speaker diarization across all 22 languages on IndicDiarBench and introduce Anuvani-Diarization, which adapts a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model to Indian conversation with uncertainty aware silver supervision. Evaluated zero shot alongside nine recent diarization systems, it reaches a duration weighted diarization error rate (DER) of 16.78% on all 1,164 recordings, the lowest of all systems we ran and second only to the best published result (16.0%), and leads the three strongest rivals in 14 of 22 languages. It matches its parent on six international benchmarks. We also show that the benchmark's utterance level annotation convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 DER points, depending on the system, and that a convention learned from other Indian transcriptions does not transfer.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(δ,ε)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $Ω\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{ΔH,L_0^2\}/ε^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,δ,ε)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey.

title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $π_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

evidence.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over π_{0.5}. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

title: Continuum Attention
abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.

title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
