title: Are You Reading the Right Thing? Rethinking Internal Signals for Prompt-Injection Detection
abstract: Several recent studies propose detecting prompt injections from a language model's internal state. However, these methods do not measure a single security property. Residual-stream probes, attention scores, role projections, exposure probes, and concept readouts may capture injection presence, recognition, information routing, or behavioral influence. It is therefore unclear what differences in prompt-injection detection performance reveal about the internal signals these methods read. We study how five representation-reading methods vary under a common structured indirect prompt-injection setup on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. We evaluate each method by how well it distinguishes injected prompts from benign controls. We then further analyze each detection method's ability to detect attacks in cases where they are successful and in cases where they are not. This helps us better assess what properties each detection method might rely on. Methods trained to detect injection presence or attack-related concepts generally separate unsuccessful injections more strongly from benign inputs, whereas attention diversion, exposure, and role-confusion-based methods separate successful injections more strongly on both models. Attention Tracker provides the strongest consistent successful injection separation, reaching 0.949 AUROC on Qwen and 0.887 on Gemma. These results suggest that signals closer to response formation may better encode information about an attack's success, and that detection performance can depend strongly on the prompt template. We share the data associated with this study at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/paper-evaluation-data-7877

title: Scaling Multilingual Mixture-of-Experts: How Language Coverage Changes Capacity and Compute Allocation
abstract: Multilingual models share capacity across languages, so adding languages can hurt performance on existing ones. Mixture-of-experts models expand this capacity with little additional per-token computation. Given this extra capacity, does adding experts reduce what each additional language costs? To answer this question, we propose a repetition-aware joint scaling law relating number of active parameters, training tokens per language, number of experts, and language coverage. Fitted on 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations, our law reduces prediction error on held-out configurations by 28% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. At matched number of active parameters and training tokens per language, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of expanding from 12 to 200 languages by 83% compared with a dense model. Our law further shows that broader language coverage favors more experts across a wider range of compute budgets, guiding capacity allocation as multilingual models scale.

title: A Diagnostic Study of World-Space Human Recovery Under High Camera Dynamics
abstract: Monocular world-space human recovery methods excel on current benchmarks, but these rarely include fast camera motion. We introduce the K-Pop stress test, broadcast dance videos that combine fast, large camera motion with dense multi-person choreography. Leading methods produce plausible per-frame meshes on these videos, yet their world-space trajectories drift far from the performers' stage positions. Through a systematic diagnosis, we show that the camera and human estimates each remain self-consistent, and that the drift appears when they are combined at mismatched scales. Each is recovered at its own scale, so a mismatch between the two can turn camera motion into human drift that grows with camera displacement and becomes severe in broadcast dance videos. We derive a closed-form correction that estimates this mismatch and applies one scale to all performers, removing the drift while keeping their relative positions in one shared world frame. It requires no retraining and works with existing backends. Combined with physical constraints, the correction yields stable world-space reconstruction for choreography modeling, scene editing, data generation, and virtual reshooting. Project page: https://chien90190.github.io/worldhmr-fastcam-website/

title: Token Ratios of the European Union's Official Languages Across Nine 2026 Tokenizers, and an Exploratory Tokenizer Transplant
abstract: Language model services count, limit and bill text in tokens, but the number of tokens needed for the same content depends on the language and on the tokenizer. We measure this token ratio relative to English for the 23 non-English official languages of the European Union on nine tokenizers of 2026: six company tokenizers run locally (OpenAI o200k, Meta Llama 3.1, Alibaba Qwen3, DeepSeek V3, Google Gemma 3, Mistral Tekken), Anthropic's Claude generation-5 tokenizer measured through its counting endpoint, and two European research tokenizers (BSC Salamandra, EuroLLM). On NTREX-128 news, mean ratios range from 1.18 (Salamandra) to 1.98 (Qwen3). Text length does not suffice to explain the gaps: Czech and Estonian are no longer than English in characters, yet need 1.40 to 2.01 times the English tokens on the seven company tokenizers. On the lowest-count company tokenizer for each language, Greek needs 2.14 times the English tokens, and Latvian, Irish and Maltese 1.81 to 1.89. Salamandra needs 13% to 30% fewer tokens than that tokenizer for Central and Eastern European, Baltic, Greek and Nordic languages, while differences for Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese and Dutch remain within about 4% and French requires 7% more tokens; EuroLLM saves at most 15%. The observed order of the eight locally run tokenizers is identical on FLORES+ and on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Claude's tokenizer gives the highest absolute count (3.08M tokens vs 1.87M for OpenAI). Finally, in an exploratory test we transplant a French-optimised tokenizer onto Qwen3-0.6B-Base: after one pass over 11 MB of professional French text, the transplanted models improve on the base model but remain behind a control adapted with its original tokenizer. These are segmentation results and one small adaptation experiment; effects on cost per task and on downstream task quality are not measured. Counts, scripts and transplant results: https://github.com/Baracoda-ai-labs/baracoda-fr. Follow-up to: T. Serval, The Invisible Language Tax, arXiv:2609.39001.

title: Q-DEIM/GKS context selection for RAG: pre-registered replication protocol (v2) on new MuSiQue questions
abstract: Pre-registration of a confirmatory replication of the study "Q-DEIM/GKS context selection for retrieval-augmented generation" (protocol v4.2) on new questions from the MuSiQue training split, with an 8B reader. The protocol (replication_protocol.md, in Italian; SHA-256 d7fb6a4813865155788a7cea4fa578358613d01b2f33e9eeab79f2debee87b02) fixes hypotheses, sample, exclusions, feasibility gate, analysis and decision rules before the training data are obtained: R1 (GKS selection improves answer F1 over cosine top-m) as gatekeeper, then Holm at 2.5% one-sided on R2 (near-duplicate filter vs cosine) and R3 (GKS vs filter), plus a secondary equivalence test (±0.005 F1). HASHES.txt lists the hashes of the sealed main study to which the replication is anchored (frozen configuration, confirmatory seal, audit-log head) and states what this deposit does and does not show. The files are restricted until the publication terms of the main study's outputs are settled; the SHA-256 above allows anyone to verify them once released.

title: Deep-Space Quantum Telemetry: Gravitational Lensing Amplification and Relativistic Entanglement Routing for Interplanetary Networks
abstract: Abstract: Interplanetary exploration, crewed lunar and Martian settlements, and deep-space astronomical observatories demand unforgeable, high-bandwidth communication fabrics immune to spoofing, eavesdropping, and catastrophic data corruption. While near-Earth quantum key distribution (QKD) is viable across low Earth orbit (LEO, h ≤ 1,000 km), extending quantum entanglement to interplanetary baselines (R ∈ [0.1, 40] AU) confronts three extreme physical barriers: (1) catastrophic geometric photon dilution governed by the inverse-square law (η_geo ∝ R^-2), dropping received single-photon fluxes below 10^-15 over astronomical baselines; (2) massive general relativistic spacetime delays, Shapiro gravitational time dilation, and solar gravitational redshift that destroy temporal coincidence windows; and (3) solar wind plasma turbulence, interplanetary coronal mass ejections, and Faraday rotation that induce severe spatial and polarization decoherence. This monograph establishes the theoretical framework, mathematical formulation, and solid-state engineering architecture for PHOENIX_DEEP, an interplanetary quantum communications network designed for deep-space sovereign exploration: (1) We model the optical amplification of the Solar Gravitational Lens (SGL) at heliocentric distances b ≥ 547.5 AU, deriving a wave-optical brightness gain µ_SGL ≈ 10^5–10^6 that converts diverging single-photon beams into coherent pencil modes; (2) We derive an exact relativistic metric incorporating post-Newtonian (PPN) solar gravitational potential and Shapiro time delays, establishing a predictive feedforward temporal coincidence gate operating across multi-hour propagation regimes; (3) We design solid-state quantum memory relay nodes deployed at Sun-Earth and Earth-Moon Lagrange points (L2, L4, L5) utilizing europium-doped yttrium silicate (Eu^3+:Y2SiO5) crystals achieving optical coherence times T_2 > 1 hour under zero-first-order-Zeeman (ZEFOZ) fields; and (4) We formulate an asynchronous device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) protocol verifying Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) Bell inequality violations (S ≥ 2.724) across astronomical distances. Our architecture achieves a continuous secret key rate exceeding 11.6 kbps at Earth-Mars quadrature (1.5 AU) and 185.6 kbps across 16-channel DWDM links, establishing an unassailable physical-layer communication infrastructure for interplanetary human civilization.

title: Benchmarking Hybrid Learning Models for Personalized Risk Classification and Prediction in Oncology
abstract: In the field of oncology, and specifically regarding prostate cancer, recent breakthroughs in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have opened fascinating possibilities for risk classification and prediction. However, moving from theoretical success to actual clinical practice remains a significant challenge. In this study, we chose to evaluate several architectures (generative, discriminant, and hybrid models) to test their real-world relevance when faced with longitudinal medical data, which is often noisy or incomplete. Our analysis does not merely measure raw performance; it seeks to understand the critical balance between statistical precision and the interpretability that clinicians require for daily decision-making. By examining the inherent strengths and limitations of each method, we developed an advanced hybrid approach designed as a genuine support tool for the patient care pathway. Our findings are particularly encouraging: these deep hybrid models significantly outperform traditional methods, showing a notable improvement of 6% to 9% in both AUC-ROC and C-index scores. Beyond these metrics, we observed a superior ability in the model to adapt to the temporal variations of patient data over time. Ultimately, our goal is to demonstrate that more refined predictions, when properly integrated into the clinical context, can simplify the decision-making process. By making these models more transparent and robust, we hope to facilitate their adoption by the medical community, leading to more personalized and effective management for patients battling prostate cancer.

title: Towards robust Graph Neural Networks: A comprehensive strategy against graph and label noise
abstract: The increasing use of graph data in emerging domains has highlighted the importance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). However, traditional GNNs are highly susceptible to both graph and label noise, leading to degraded and unstable performance under noisy conditions. To address this challenge, we propose a R obust S tructure and L abel D enoising G raph N eural N etwork (RSLD-GNN) that jointly refines graph structure and node labels while decoupling their optimization. RSLD-GNN performs structural refinement by combining dynamic and static graph augmentation with knowledge distillation, enabling robust exploration and stabilization of the graph structure. For label denoising, a detached label head isolates label correction from the main computational graph, reducing the influence of structural noise on label refinement and generating more reliable pseudo-labels. These two refinement processes are further connected through mutual regularization: loss-based edge reweighting suppresses connections involving nodes with potentially noisy labels, while the resulting cleaner structure facilitates more reliable label propagation. All modules are pretrained under controlled noise to reduce sensitivity to noise during early optimization. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets under single-graph, single-label, and mixed-noise settings show that RSLD-GNN ranks first in 69 of 80 noisy evaluation settings while remaining competitive on clean datasets.

title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.

title: In-Context Batch Black-box Optimization via Flow Matching
abstract: Batch black-box optimization is important for expensive systems where many candidates can be evaluated in parallel, yet only a few rounds of evaluation are affordable. In this regime, effective batch construction must identify multiple promising regions while avoiding redundant evaluations, and conventional Bayesian optimization can require increasingly difficult batch-selection procedures as the batch size grows. We introduce Flow Matching for Thompson-Sampling Refinement (FMTR), an amortized approach that learns offline a continuous, history-conditioned proposal distribution from which variable-size batches can be sampled. FMTR is trained offline by conditional flow matching on Thompson-sampling argmaxes refined toward high-value regions via a horizon-dependent Langevin pushforward map, adapting the exploration-exploitation tradeoff over the optimization horizon. At test time, the model parameters remain fixed and batch generation requires neither task-specific surrogate refitting nor numerical acquisition optimization. FMTR achieves strong performance against batch BO and in-context baselines on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, while substantially reducing the computational cost of batch selection.

title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
abstract: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

title: Mapping Arctic Polynyas from Sea Ice Concentration Data Using Hierarchical Partitioning and Differentiated Region Growing: Sensitivity to Threshold and Product Choices
abstract: Accurately delineating Arctic coastal polynyas from sea ice concentration data remains challenging because of complex coastal geometry and spatially heterogeneous ice conditions. We develop a daily sea ice concentration (SIC) mapping framework based on hierarchical partitioning, connected-component analysis, and differentiated region growing for polynya and open-water regions. Applied to September-May ice seasons from 2002/03 to 2024/25, the framework achieves a mean overall accuracy of 96.74% and a mean kappa coefficient of 0.93 in the 63-scene visual assessment. Sensitivity experiments reveal a consistent pattern: the absolute magnitude of SIC-defined polynya extent is strongly configuration-dependent, whereas major temporal features are comparatively more stable. Relative to a 75% upper SIC threshold, seasonal extent integrals differ by 13.48%, 32.47%, and 65.04% at thresholds of 80%, 85%, and 90%, respectively, while the broad interannual structure remains recognizable. The response is also strongly regional and seasonal, with the largest threshold sensitivity in the Central Arctic Ocean, very weak sensitivity in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and greater pan-Arctic curve separation from January onward. At an 80% threshold, product-comparison MAPE is 68.19% between the 6.25 and 25 km products and 11.47% between the 12.5 and 25 km products under their respective comparison periods and reference definitions. Regional product disagreement is likewise heterogeneous. Together, these results show that reproducible long-term polynya monitoring requires a fixed and explicitly documented combination of SIC product, threshold, and spatial classification rules, while broad temporal patterns can remain informative even when absolute extent differs substantially.

title: Quantum LDPC Codes from Polynomial Minors
abstract: We construct quantum codes from codewords of a cyclic code and the minors of a polynomial matrix. The construction uses a two-row, three-column matrix whose minors yield a second matrix satisfying the CSS orthogonality condition. We derive the code dimension from the greatest common divisors of the entries and minors, with a simplified formula for odd lifting factors. A residue characterization identifies additional common factors of the minors and leads to a method for controlling the dimension through polynomial selection. We also give a condition for changing the minor generator without changing the code. Explicit polynomial constructions yield 13 quantum codes with verified minimum distances, including a $[[255,80,12]]$ code of rate $80/255$.

title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
abstract: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.

title: A Two-Level Clinical Novelty Prioritization Framework for Disease Trajectories Discovered from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
abstract: Graph-based analysis of electronic health records (EHRs) yields disease-trajectory catalogs, but structural support does not establish semantic novelty. We present a two-level framework to prioritize 99,527 branching motifs previously discovered by an upstream patient-disjoint, train-only MIMIC-IV v3.1 pipeline and frozen after validation-based catalog selection. The framework separates path-level and node-to-endpoint semantic sparsity from reliability-adjusted clinical priority. Three deterministic textualizations per motif or node-target pair were embedded with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 and calibrated against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references using mean top-20 cosine distance. Positive recombination occurred in 8.63% of motifs and had negligible effect on global ranking, whereas specificity and support/GNN reliability terms changed clinical-priority ordering. Robustness analyses across neighbor counts, templates, encoders, generic-label taxonomies, score settings, PrimeKG, and corrected density-based RND showed that broad ordering was more stable than hard top-k membership. A semantic-dose analysis did not support a monotonic relation between score and forecasting benefit after endpoint and token-count adjustment (1.96 days per SD; 95% CI, -0.75 to 4.68). In the frozen catalog-q90 high-semantic subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting reduced conditional event-time MAE by 20.1 days (95% CI, 13.3-27.0) and sMAPE by 2.37 percentage points (95% CI, 1.81-2.93), while discrimination and endpoint-ranking differences were inconclusive. Corrected RND showed low tail agreement with the primary score (Spearman rho = 0.430; q90 Jaccard = 0.125) despite a similar aggregate timing association. These findings support representation-aware, uncertainty-aware literature-relative prioritization of discovered trajectories rather than causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty.

title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

title: RAC: A Relational Agent Contract for Constraint-Governed Engineering Tasks
abstract: Engineering agents must produce artifacts that satisfy exact, coupled constraints. Existing solutions often require agents to make semantic decisions and also derive consequences such as precise geometry or timing from those decisions, leading to failures in constraint-governed engineering tasks. In this paper, we introduce RAC, a harness-agnostic contract for the action and feedback layer of engineering agents. It specifies authoritative observations, semantic actions, tool-based realization, independent verification, and repair evidence. The agent decides which relations an artifact should satisfy; specialized tools derive their concrete consequences. On PCB placement, routing, and repair tasks, RAC achieves the highest clean-pass rate for all nine evaluated models, averaging 90.9%, compared with 74.0% for the strongest baseline, requirements-only delegation. In job-shop scheduling, direct relational actions achieve 96.3% quality pass versus 59.6% for code-mediated delivery with access to the same scheduling backend. Our evaluations on 141 embedded-code tasks across four microcontroller identify the action contract as a source of agent capability: preserving semantic control while delegating mechanically derivable outputs improves the reliability of constrained artifacts.

title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.

title: Choosing the Number of Attention Heads from Intrinsic Dimension: A Small-Scale Study
abstract: The number of attention heads in a transformer is usually set by convention or grid search. We test a simple heuristic for setting it in advance: estimate the intrinsic dimension of token representations without labels, and use roughly that many heads. We estimate intrinsic dimension with a nested-dropout VAE trained on DistilBERT embeddings of WikiText-2, choosing the KL weight at the knee of the VAE's rate-distortion curve rather than by hand. This gives $k^*=9.2$ (95% CI [8.6, 9.8]). In a small 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, 10 heads and 32 heads are statistically equivalent on SST-2 and on MRPC (paired TOST over 10 seeds, $\pm1$ point margin), with 69% fewer attention parameters for the 10-head model. Training 10 heads from the start also slightly outperforms training 32 heads and pruning to 10 (0.6 points, $p=0.008$). The evidence is narrow: two classification tasks, one small architecture, no pretrained models, and no formal link between intrinsic dimension and head count. We present the result as a practical heuristic worth testing at larger scale, not as a general principle.

title: LWM-TF: A Wireless Foundation Model on 5G NR Time-Frequency Resource Grids
abstract: Received OFDM grids preserve both pilot and payload observations, yet wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained on them. We introduce LWM-TF, a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on complex 5G NR uplink grids taken after the FFT and before channel estimation. Each block attends first across OFDM symbols and then across resource blocks and receive antennas, and the mask follows the same two axes. Because the payload phase is unpredictable, the model reconstructs the normalized log-power of each masked token and predicts its scale separately; ablations show that the two terms are complementary and that this target outperforms complex-signal reconstruction. The encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) slots from a 10^6-slot dataset simulated with the NR transmit chain under various channel conditions. With the encoder frozen, linear probes classify modulation, predict CRC success, and detect UE mobility. On a separately generated test set, 16 labeled slots per class give 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC area under the ROC curve (AUROC), and 0.73 mobility AUROC, ahead of a supervised CNN on every paired draw. With 10,000 labels the probes reach 0.94, 0.96, and 0.92, well above engineered receiver statistics, and detect mobility where the CNN stays at chance. Without any impairment labels, distances in the frozen feature space flag unseen waveform impairments with 0.78 macro AUROC, against 0.68 for receiver statistics. A single pre-trained encoder thus provides receiver features that transfer across tasks, most strongly when labels are scarce.

title: DocuMind AI: A Document-Powered Question Answering System Using Semantic Retrieval
abstract: Users often need answers from lengthy documents without knowing the exact terms used in the source. DocuMind AI is a document question-answering prototype that combines semantic retrieval with large language model generation. It accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT, and Markdown files, extracts and splits their text, creates embeddings using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and indexes the chunks in FAISS. For each question, relevant chunks are supplied to ChatGroq using llama-3.3-70b-versatile. The Streamlit interface includes answer-length preferences, eight language options, recent conversation context, and dark/light modes. Project-reported preliminary evaluation found relevant content in the top three retrieved chunks for 87% of 30 factual questions and correct abstention on 19 of 20 out-of-context questions. These results come from small samples, and the test documentation is incomplete; they should not be treated as general performance guarantees. The prototype demonstrates a document-grounded interaction workflow while retaining limitations in extraction quality, retrieval coverage, multilingual reliability, and answer attribution.

title: Computational Bounds for f -Routing
abstract: The f-routing protocol is a leading candidate for quantum position verification, but security guarantees for explicit functions remain limited. We prove unconditional resource lower bounds for uniform attackers; our new techniques bypass communication-complexity bounds central to previous works, which are inherently at most linear in the input length. We show that, for input length n and sufficiently small constant ε > 0, a uniformly generated strategy using q qubits and having description length poly(q), with success probability at least 1 − ε on every input, implies the following computational bounds on f: 1. If the strategies are arbitrary quantum channels, then f ∈ QSZK(poly(nq)), where QSZK(T ) is the class of languages having quantum statistical zero knowledge proofs in which the verifier runs in time T (and the simulator in time poly(T )). 2. If the strategies are explicit Pauli-sparse unitaries on q qubits that have at most s nonzero Pauli coefficients, then f ∈ DTIME(poly(nqs)). 3. If the strategies are Clifford+T circuits using at most t magic gates, then f ∈ DTIME(poly(nq2t)). Time and space hierarchies then yield explicit functions secure against polynomial and even quasipolynomial qubits q under our computational restrictions. These bounds exceed the q ≤ log n bound of [BCS22] for inner product function f = IP, at the cost of restricting adversarial computation and increasing honest evaluation complexity.

title: Attention-based and contrastive deep learning models for real-time anomaly detection in Edge-IIoT networks
abstract: The rapid expansion of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) systems has increased the cyber-attack surface of critical infrastructure, requiring intrusion detection systems (IDS) that are accurate, robust, and efficient under resource-constrained edge environments. Traditional approaches suffer from limited generalization, poor handling of class imbalance, and lack of statistical reliability and interpretability. This paper proposes a modular deep learning framework integrating TabTransformer, Variational Autoencoder, and contrastive learning, combined through multi-trial training (N = 10), statistical aggregation, and F1-weighted ensemble fusion. Experiments on the Edge-IIoTset dataset ( $$\approx $$ 1.9M samples, 15 classes) achieve 97.60% accuracy and 83.42% F1-score, with multi-trial aggregation reducing the uncertainty associated with single-run reporting. From a computational perspective, training is performed using large-batch optimization (batch size = 16,384) with early stopping (patience = 50), while inference requires a single forward pass per model followed by constant-time fusion. The framework operates on compact tabular inputs ( $$\approx $$ 96 features), resulting in a lightweight memory footprint (on the order of a few megabytes per model) and enabling efficient deployment. The inference pipeline processes batches in a few milliseconds on GPU-class hardware, ensuring real-time responsiveness for high-throughput IIoT traffic streams while maintaining low computational overhead and energy demand. Ablation analysis shows that removing ensemble fusion reduces F1-score by approximately 1%:2%, while eliminating multi-trial aggregation significantly increases variance, highlighting the importance of statistical robustness. Furthermore, SHAP-based explainable AI (XAI) provides insight into feature-level contributions, enhancing transparency and supporting human-in-the-loop security operations. Overall, the proposed framework achieves a balanced trade-off between predictive performance and computational efficiency, delivering a reproducible, interpretable, and deployment-oriented IDS solution for real-time IIoT environments. Practical deployment considerations, including model export to ONNX format and quantization for edge hardware, are outlined as immediate next steps.

title: Cultural value configurations and guests’ evaluations of AI-enabled service technologies
abstract: As Artificial Intelligence reshapes hospitality service delivery, understanding how culturally diverse guests evaluate AI-enabled encounters is critical. This study examines how cultural value configurations shape evaluations of service robots in hotels. Cultural value configurations are coherent combinations of orientations that jointly influence how individuals interpret and assess service encounters. Using more than 3000 robot-related hotel reviews from guests across 77 countries, we integrate Hofstede’s dimensions with Schwartz’s value theory to explain cross-cultural differences in sentiment. title: monoprop: Scaling Pauli and Majorana propagation via Anticommutation Indices
abstract: We introduce monoprop, an open-source, massively parallel operator-propagation framework for fermion and qubit bases. For $N$ qubits or modes, existing codes represent each of the $K$ tracked operator terms (Pauli strings or products of Majorana operators) as a $2N$-bit string, testing each for anticommutation with the gate at $O(KN)$ cost per gate. Here, we introduce the anticommutation index which rapidly looks up the terms anticommuting with a gate. A local gate changes only the terms that touch its sites, and when terms are truncated to act on few sites, only a fraction $\sim1/N$ touch any given qubit or mode, and we use this to prove the time per gate scales as $O(K/N)$. This counterintuitive result tells us that for a fixed number of terms, increasing the number of sites can make things faster. We demonstrate this numerically, and show monoprop scales almost ideally to 8192 cores, tracking $9.5\times10^{10}$ terms. Beyond propagation, we present memory-efficient surrogate graphs, which record one propagation and replay it at new angles, for fast energy re-estimation and parameter gradients, and an efficient method for finding energy-minimising gates and optimal angles for simulating adaptive quantum-chemistry circuits.

title: Nodal nematic superconductivity in moiré graphene
abstract: Unconventional superconductivity can emerge in various forms in strongly correlated systems. Historically, the most extensively studied examples include nodal and triplet pairing, which were experimentally detected in cuprates and superfluid helium-3, respectively. Beyond these canonical cases, there are also nematic superconductors, in which the rotational symmetry of the lattice is broken in the superconducting state. While there are several examples of nematic superconductors whose pairing emerges inside a preexisting nematic normal state, experimental evidence for superconducting states that intrinsically break rotational symmetry on their own has been exceedingly scarce. Here, we report the experimental realization and identification of an intrinsic multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG). By integrating tunneling spectroscopy with quantum transport measurements, we directly probe the symmetry of low-energy superconducting quasiparticles. Deep inside the superconducting state, we observe a pronounced two-fold anisotropy in the zero-bias tunneling conductance under an in-plane magnetic field, which is strongly suppressed together with superconductivity as the temperature or perpendicular magnetic field is increased. Remarkably, the major axis of anisotropy rotates by up to 90^{circ} across the superconducting dome, indicating an intrinsic, field- and density-tunable symmetry of the low-energy excitations. These behaviors imply a nodal superconducting state in MATTG that spontaneously breaks the six-fold rotational symmetry of the moiré superlattice. Our results establish moiré graphene as a versatile platform for realizing and interrogating nodal nematic superconductivity, opening a new avenue for exploring unconventional symmetry-breaking superconducting states in two-dimensional materials.

title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
abstract: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.

title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents
abstract: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.

title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

title: Graph Additive Models disentangling feature, topology, and interactions
abstract: Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as effective, interpretable-by-design architectures for graph learning. They achieve transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with simple distance-based reweighting. However, GNANs have three limitations. First, node-wise relevance scores aggregate information from all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones. Second, topology is represented only through shortest-path distances, so structurally distinct graphs may share identical distance profiles. Third, feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects in a single rescalable term. We introduce AMIGA, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes each node contribution into three additive channels: feature, structure, and feature-structure interaction. The channels are centered around a graph-balanced training baseline, making the decomposition well-defined and unique under the chosen reference distribution. Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, AMIGA outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap with standard black-box GNNs. Because each channel is centered and assigned to a single node, AMIGA produces node-local explanations that reconstruct the model output exactly and support interpretation at multiple levels of granularity.

title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

title: Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness
abstract: Backdoor attacks on deep neural networks are commonly evaluated by attack success rate and benign accuracy, yet their stealthiness remains inconsistently defined and measured. Existing work often studies only one observable aspect of stealthiness, such as trigger imperceptibility, feature-space separability, parameter-space concentration, or evasion of particular defenses. This creates a fragmented picture: an attack may appear stealthy under one metric while leaving conspicuous footprints elsewhere. This paper presents a tri-space measurement study of backdoor stealthiness in image classification. We distinguish latent stealthiness---the ideal but unobservable difficulty of distinguishing a backdoored system from a benign one---from measurable footprints in three spaces: input, feature, and parameter space. Under this framework, we evaluate representative backdoor attacks across four datasets and three model architectures using a broad suite of footprint metrics. Our results show that stealthiness is not monolithic: attacks that are quiet in one space are often loud in another, and existing attacks rarely achieve consistently small footprints across all three spaces. We further analyze agreement and disagreement among stealthiness metrics and study how footprint measurements interact with attack success rate. Based on observed blind spots in existing measurements, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: Class-Specific Davies--Bouldin Index (CDBI), which captures class-conditional feature overlap, and TAC--UCLC Product (TUP), which identifies channels that are both trigger-responsive and downstream influential. These metrics are intended to augment, not replace, the broader measurement suite. Finally, we provide practical guidance for future stealthiness evaluations.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.

We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.

title: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills
abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.

title: When does tail-risk optimization change a quantum gate? An equivalence boundary for mean and CVaR control
abstract: Control pulses for quantum gates are normally optimized for the error averaged over noise. Fault tolerance, however, is sensitive to the worst gates, which suggests optimizing the tail of the error distribution instead. Doing so is costly, since only a small fraction of the samples lies in the tail, and it is not known in advance whether the resulting pulse will differ from the one that minimizes the mean. We show that for Gaussian noise entering the gate linearly it does not: the error distributions of all pulses differ only by a scale factor, so the pulse with the smallest mean error is also optimal for every monotone measure of tail risk. In simulations of a transmon qubit, hundreds of candidate pulses per setting contain essentially no clearly separated pair that the mean and the tail rank differently below an accumulated phase variance of about 0.05. The two objectives separate once the optimized pulse retains error of second order in the noise. The tail-optimal gate then carries a coherent offset that lowers its nominal fidelity but cancels the quadratic error of the worst noise realizations. Its advantage scales as the square of the ratio of quadratic to linear error, and we give the coefficient in closed form. Noise memory and rare relaxation events change the shape of the tail, in quantitative agreement with our predictions, but alter the optimal pulse only when the pulse can act on the channel involved. Because the size of the advantage can be estimated from the mean-optimal gate, one can decide whether tail optimization is worth its cost before running it.

title: Query-Relative Walsh Compression: Sharp Punctured Norms and Signed Bent-Orbit Recovery
abstract: For signed differences of measures on \(\mathbb F_2^m\), we determine sharp comparisons between total variation and punctured (zero-frequency-deleted) Walsh \(L^p\) spectra. For every \(m\) and \(1\le p\le2\), the optimal constant is \(\Lambda_{m,p}=2^{m/p-1}\). For all dimensions \(m\le5\) we also give analytical sharp formulas throughout \(2\le p\le\infty\); in particular the five-bit formula is \(\Lambda_{5,p}=\frac{32^{1/p-1}}2(16\cdot4^q+12\cdot8^q)^{1/q}\), where \(q=p/(p-1)\). The result is a continuous-exponent punctured-norm theorem, not a claim that the classical five-bit endpoint value 160 or the underlying Boolean spectral catalogues were first discovered here. For observations of a known quadratic bent-function translation/sign orbit, exact identification is equivalent to affine spanning by sampled frequencies. The first-order Reed–Muller code determines optimal worst-case sign-error, erasure and Euclidean-noise thresholds. We also identify a sharp six-bit bent regime for \(p\ge2.5590297\ldots\) and an explicit counterexample to bent optimality for \(2\le p<2.1269266\ldots\); the intermediate regime remains unresolved. Sharpness for arbitrary signed differences is not automatically claimed for the more restricted class of characteristic-function dependence defects.

title: PARALLEL CORPORA AND NEURAL MODELS FOR THE UZBEK LANGUAGE: CURRENT STATE AND DEVELOPMENT PATHS
abstract: This article examines the role of parallel corpora in developing neural machine translation for the Uzbek language. The concept of a parallel corpus is analysed, existing resources for Uzbek are reviewed, and methodological principles of corpus construction are formulated: representativeness, alignment quality, metadata annotation, and licensing. The article analyses how corpus characteristics affect neural model behaviour — error types observed in English–Uzbek MT are correlated with corpus gaps. Development paths are proposed: national corpus programs, domain-specific corpora, community-driven collection, and post-editing data feedback loops. The conclusion argues that corpus construction is the single most effective investment for improving Uzbek MT quality, and that a coordinated national effort, combining academic, governmental, and community resources, is needed to move Uzbek from low-resource to medium-resource status.

title: Optimal Fusion of Delayed Price Feeds: Filtering, Identification, Model Choice and Surveillance
abstract: The information value of a price feed depends on its delay, noise persistence, and other feeds' histories. We study estimation, identification and surveillance for a Gaussian random walk observed through independent AR(1) feed noises with common persistence and integer delays. The exact steady-state filtering error for finitely many feeds reduces to scalar fractional-linear maps. Closed forms make covariance evaluation depend on the count of distinct ages rather than their magnitude; a recursion recovers the conditional mean. Every additional independent feed with finite delay has strictly positive information value, and increasing an individual feed's delay or noise variance strictly raises optimal mean-square error. For two feeds, we derive the stale stream's exact value and exponential decay with excess delay. An expansion near unit persistence gives a sufficient condition for an interior error maximum. Joint delay–persistence limits do not commute: streams can remain informative at large delays with sufficiently persistent noise. Gaussian quadratic-form concentration yields a uniform finite-sample bound for cross-covariance estimates and a condition for exact relative-delay recovery. Under compatible unanchored initial laws, common delay shifts preserve the observation law while changing current-price uncertainty; unbounded shifts preclude finite-width intervals with positive uniform coverage, whereas a bounded age bracket yields a conditional minimax risk bound. On a comparison graph, changes affecting at most s feeds are uniformly identifiable if and only if every connected component contains more than 2s vertices. Majority centering supplies stable recovery, and the concentration bound gives a finite-sample attribution guarantee across homogeneous segments. We formulate model comparison on a common observation space, distinguish exact Gaussian filtering from the interacting multiple model approximation, and construct an anytime-valid likelihood surveillance rule over a declared null family. Proofs specify initialization, support and information assumptions required by each guarantee. Independent scalar and augmented-state implementations, randomized configurations and synthetic experiments check the formulas.

title: KI-kompasset: Et strategisk verktøy for å navigere KI-implementering
abstract: Når KI bygges inn i beslutningssystemer kan det forsterke gode valg, men også skalere konsekvensene av dårlige. Organisasjoner behandler ofte KI-implementering som et teknisk problem, men det er i stor grad et strategisk spørsmål om verdiforslag og ansvarsfordeling. Hvilke mål skal KI optimaliseres mot, og hvilke beslutninger bør vi ikke delegere bort? I denne artikkelen presenteres KI-kompasset, et verktøy som definerer fire idealtypiske roller for KI i ulike beslutningsprosesser. Ledere må først diagnostisere beslutningstypen, deretter velge KI-rolle. Kompasset hjelper ledere med diagnose slik at KI-satsninger underbygger i stedet for undergraver organisasjonens egen strategi og dens kunders opplevde verdiforslag. ENGLISH ABSTRACT The AI ​​Compass: A Strategic Tool for Navigating AI Implementation Integrated into decision systems, AI can amplify both good and bad decision-making. Organizations often treat AI implementation as a technical issue, yet it is largely a strategic question of value proposition and accountability. Which goals should AI optimize, and which decisions should not be delegated? We present the AI Compass, which defines four ideal-typical roles for AI in decision processes. Managers must first diagnose the decision type, then choose AI's role. The compass supports this diagnosis so that AI initiatives reinforce rather than undermine the organization's strategy and its customers' perceived value proposition.

title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.

title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

title: Seeing at the Edge: Energy Characterization of Vision-Language Model Inference on Edge Platforms
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.

title: A particle swarm optimization with a reduced-subspace trust-region safeguard for contact-rich controller tuning
abstract: Contact-rich robotic insertion is challenging because uncertainty in alignment, friction, and contact conditions can lead to unsuccessful assembly, excessive contact forces, and jamming. Designing a reliable controller therefore requires balancing insertion performance, robustness, and recovery from unexpected contact. In this paper, we propose PSO+TR, a derivative-free optimization (DFO) method that combines the exploratory search of particle swarm optimization (PSO) with a trust-region (TR) procedure for local refinement to improve the search process when progress stagnates. We apply the method to derivative-free policy optimization of an interpretable robotic insertion controller, jointly tuning its motion, feedback, and recovery parameters while preserving its predefined control structure. The proposed approach is evaluated on 93 eligible benchmark problems from the bound-constrained programs (BCP) collection and a synthetic contact-rich planar insertion task under uncertain operating conditions. Three random seeds per benchmark problem yield 279 matched problem--seed instances per method. PSO+TR reaches the prescribed target on 228 of these instances (81.72\%), the highest observed target-attainment rate among the five compared methods, which also include PSO, randomized black-box optimization (VRBBO), matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES), and differential evolution (DE). Across eight robotic optimizer seeds, the deployed controller-selection pipeline achieves 97.78\% completion under development conditions and 58.00\% under withheld stress conditions, compared with 91.22\% and 31.12\%, respectively, for the fixed staged controller. The stress violation rate is reduced from 20.69\% to 2.19\%. These findings support combining global and local search for DFO and structured contact-rich controller tuning. The synthetic planar results require validation on physical robots.

In this paper, we propose PSO+TR, a derivative-free optimization (DFO) method that combines the exploratory search of particle swarm optimization (PSO) with a trust-region (TR) procedure for local refinement to improve the search process when progress stagnates. We apply the method to derivative-free policy optimization of an interpretable robotic insertion controller, jointly tuning its motion, feedback, and recovery parameters while preserving its predefined control structure. The proposed approach is evaluated on 93 eligible benchmark problems from the bound-constrained programs (BCP) collection and a synthetic contact-rich planar insertion task under uncertain operating conditions. Three random seeds per benchmark problem yield 279 matched problem--seed instances per method. PSO+TR reaches the prescribed target on 228 of these instances (81.72\%), the highest observed target-attainment rate among the five compared methods, which also include PSO, randomized black-box optimization (VRBBO), matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES), and differential evolution (DE). Across eight robotic optimizer seeds, the deployed controller-selection pipeline achieves 97.78\% completion under development conditions and 58.00\% under withheld stress conditions, compared with 91.22\% and 31.12\%, respectively, for the fixed staged controller. The stress violation rate is reduced from 20.69\% to 2.19\%. These findings support combining global and local search for DFO and structured contact-rich controller tuning. The synthetic planar results require validation on physical robots.

title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
abstract: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/

title: Value-Guided Repulsion for Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Drifting models have emerged as a highly efficient and stable paradigm for policy design in offline reinforcement learning (RL). However, standard drift policies determine repulsion solely from geometric relationships among generated actions and therefore cannot distinguish them by expected value. To address this limitation, we introduce Value-Guided Repulsion Q-Learning (VRQL) to integrate action value estimates into the particle interaction field. For each state, VRQL combines geometric kernel distance with a normalized Q value scaling. This mechanism assigns greater repulsive influence to particles with lower values while strictly retaining attraction toward behavior action. Consequently, this value-guided interaction field aligns behavior regularization with policy improvement without adding an auxiliary behavior model stage. On 50 OGBench task configurations and 6 D4RL AntMaze configurations, VRQL demonstrates highly competitive performance against established baselines, suggesting that value-guided particle interaction is an effective method for offline RL.

title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.

title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy
abstract: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.

title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES
abstract: Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.
